title.en: The Gods of the Haitian Mountains: a Nursery Lesson in Mythology
title.zh: 海地群山之神：神話啟蒙課

source.work: William B. Seabrook, 'The Magic Island' (1929), ch. I-III 'The Voodoo Rites' (Louis's theology lessons under the palms)

summary.en: Under the trees Louis taught the names and attributes of the many Voodoo gods: Papa Legba, guardian of the gates, the most benevolent; Damballa Oueddo, wisest and most powerful, whose symbol was the serpent; Loco, god of the forests; Agoue, god of the sea; Maîtresse Ezilee, who was the mild Blessed Virgin Mary; Ogoun Badagris, the bloody dreadful, 'One whose voice was thunder' — dozens of them, like a nursery lesson in Greek mythology, except that to Louis these were not myths, they were more real than he or the white visitor who sat listening.
summary.zh: 樹蔭下，路易教他眾多伏都神的名號與職司：守門最仁厚的雷格巴老爹；智慧至高、以蛇為象的丹巴拉·維多；森林之神洛科；海神阿古埃；即是溫柔聖母的埃稀麗女神；以及『聲如雷霆』的嗜血可怖者奧貢·巴達格里斯——神名以十計，如一堂希臘神話啟蒙課；只是在路易眼中，這些不是神話，而是比他、比那位白人聽者更真實的存在。

sensitivity.note: Seabrook's 1929 popular-ethnography, sensational in places but based on participant observation with named informants (Louis, Maman Celie, Papa Theodore); the loa theology here is teaching-level content, not initiatory knowledge. Living religion: nothing beyond the published record reproduced.

passages.text: Louis and Seabrook began to go wandering in the hills together and sitting under trees, where he would tell of the names and attributes of the many Voodoo gods: Papa Legba, guardian of the gates, who was the most benevolent; Damballa Oueddo, wisest and most powerful, whose symbol was the serpent; Loco, god of the forests; Agoue, god of the sea; Maîtresse Ezilee, who was the mild Blessed Virgin Mary; Ogoun Badagris, the bloody dreadful One whose voice was thunder.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Seabrook, The Magic Island, ch. I (1929); not verbatim.

passages.text: There were dozens of them, it seemed. It was like a nursery lesson in Greek mythology, except that to Louis these were not myths — they were more real than he or Seabrook. No need to catalogue all their names: most of them fell naturally into the record later. Perhaps before the book was ended a table of theological Voodoo statistics might be compiled, but it would not be as congenial a task as sitting with Louis under a palm tree.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Seabrook, ch. I (1929); not verbatim.

title.en: Good Friday: Damballa Bows His Hooded Head
title.zh: 受難日：丹巴拉低垂蛇首

source.work: William B. Seabrook, 'The Magic Island' (1929), ch. II 'The Way Is Opened and Closed' (the Good Friday burial of the altars)

summary.en: The Christian flute that once piped first-communion hymns now piped pagan melodies to Legba and the serpent gods — and its first-communion papers lay with ancient thunderstones on a Voodoo altar. But late in a Holy Week Seabrook returned to see that same altar stripped of all its sacred objects, Christian and pagan together, laid as if dead in rows upon the ground, covered with palm fronds, to remain thus buried as Lord Jesus was until the Easter resurrection morn: during Golgotha's tragedy even the great Voodoo serpent-god Damballa must bow his hooded head — and with the half million Voodoo altars in Haiti, on each succeeding anniversary, it was the same.
summary.zh: 曾奏初領聖體聖歌的笛子，如今為雷格巴與蛇神吹起異教的曲子；初領聖禮的紙片，與遠古雷石同置於伏都祭壇之上。然而聖週將盡，主人再訪時只見同一祭壇已被剝空——基督徒與異教聖物一同橫陳如死者，覆以棕櫚枝，如主耶穌般安眠，直待復活節清晨：在各各他受難之日，連偉大的伏都蛇神丹巴拉也須低垂其蛇首——海地五十萬座伏都祭壇，年年如此。

sensitivity.note: Recorded description of syncretic Holy Week practice; living religion documented from the published 1929 account.

passages.text: Ye patient, pious, and mildly tolerant priests of Croix des Bouquets — would it have caused you pangs to know that the flute you once gave Louis from the goodness of your hearts, which your own consecrated hands taught him to play, was now piping pagan melodies to Legba, serpent gods, and peacocks; to know that his pretty first-communion papers, engraved in the shadow of Saint Sulpice and brought in Christian vessels across the seas, now lay with ancient thunderstones upon a Voodoo altar?
passages.note: Paraphrase of Seabrook, The Magic Island, ch. II (1929); not verbatim.

passages.text: If so, your pious pangs would have been in part assuaged could you have seen that selfsame altar as Seabrook chanced to return and see it long afterward, late in a Holy Week: all its sacred objects, Christian and pagan together, were stripped from it on the evening of Good Friday, laid as if dead in rows before it upon the ground and covered over with palm fronds, to remain thus buried as Lord Jesus was until the Easter resurrection morn.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Seabrook, ch. II (1929); not verbatim.

passages.text: During Golgotha's tragedy, even the great Voodoo serpent-god Damballa must bow his hooded head. And with the half million Voodoo altars in Haiti, it was and has been, so Seabrook was told, on each succeeding anniversary the same. Here are deep matters, not easily to be dismissed by crying blasphemy.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Seabrook, ch. II (1929); not verbatim.

source.work: William B. Seabrook, 'The Magic Island' (1929), ch. on the ceremony — the Damballa ritual march (papaloi with asson, serpent flags, mamaloi in scarlet)

summary.en: The drums began a new, less deafening rhythm — the Damballa ritual march. The celebrants approached processionally, singing, from the mystery house: at the head the papaloi, blue-overalled, bare-footed, a surplice on his shoulders and a red turban on his head, waving before him the asson, a gourd-rattle wound round with snake-vertebrae; two young women at his right and left holding aloft, crossed above his head, two flags sewn with serpentine and cabalistic symbols in glittering metallic beads; a young man bearing aloft a sword on his upstretched palms; the mamaloi in a scarlet robe and feathered headdress revolving as she progressed in a sort of dervish dance; then two by two, a chorus of twenty or more women robed in white, chanting as they marched: 'Damballa Oueddo, nous p'vinid' — 'Oh, Serpent God, we come.'
summary.zh: 鼓聲轉入一段不再震耳的節奏——丹巴拉儀仗進行曲。祭眾自神秘之屋列隊而來，且行且歌：領頭的老祭司身著藍布工裝、赤足，肩披白衣、頭纏紅巾，搖動纏繞蛇脊的葫蘆鈴；左右二女高擎繡有蛇紋符號、金屬珠片閃光的雙旗，交叉於其頭上；一少年雙手平托長劍；猩紅袍、羽冠的女祭司旋轉如旋舞；其後二十餘白衣女子兩兩成列，白布纏頭，且行且唱：『丹巴拉·維多，我們來了。』

sensitivity.note: Seabrook's footnote is kept in spirit: the ceremony as described is a new formalized ritual grown from the earliest slave-days merging of African cults, not the unchanged African rite. Published description only; living practice not reproduced beyond it.

passages.text: The drums began a new, less deafening rhythm: it was the Damballa ritual march. The celebrants approached, processionally, singing, from the mystery house. At the head came the papaloi, an old man, blue-overalled, bare-footed, but with a surplice over his shoulders and a red turban on his head, waving before him the asson, a gourd-rattle wound round with snake-vertebrae. At his right and left, keeping pace with him, two young women held aloft, crossed above his head, two flags on which were serpentine and cabalistic symbols, sewn on with metallic, glittering beads.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Seabrook, The Magic Island (1929); not verbatim.

passages.text: Behind him marched a young man bearing aloft, horizontally on his upstretched palms, a sword; and next the mamaloi, a woman in a scarlet robe and feathered headdress, who revolved as she progressed in a sort of dervish dance; next came marching, two and two, a chorus of twenty or more women robed in white, with white cloths wound bandana-wise on their heads, and as they slowly marched they chanted: 'Damballa Oueddo, nous p'vinid' — which would be best translated, 'Oh, Serpent God, we come.'

Seabrook's own note records what the practitioners' caution would add: although Damballa, the ancient African serpent god, remains enthroned as its central figure, this Voodoo ceremony is not the old traditional ritual brought over from Africa, but rather a gradually formalized new ritual which sprang from the merging, in earliest slave days, of the African cults with the circumstances of the new world.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Seabrook (1929), footnote paraphrased; not verbatim.

title.en: The Zombies of Hasco: Ti Joseph's Cane Gang, 1918
title.zh: 哈斯科的還魂屍：小約瑟夫的蔗田隊

texts.period: Haitian legend, event of 1918; recorded 1927-1929; published 2024 (published 2026)

source.work: William B. Seabrook, 'The Magic Island' (1929), ch. 'Black Sorcery' — the Hasco story told by Constant Polynice

summary.en: In the big cane season of 1918 the Haitian-American Sugar Company offered a bonus for new workers, and one morning old headman Ti Joseph of Colombier appeared leading a band of ragged creatures who shuffled behind him staring dumbly like people walking in a daze, making no reply when asked their names. They were poor unhappy zombies, Joseph and his wife Croyance had dragged them from their peaceful graves to slave for him in the sun — and everyone knows the zombies must never be permitted to taste salt or meat, so Croyance tended two pots, theirs flat, tasteless, and unseasoned.
summary.zh: 一九一八年蔗季，海地美糖公司懸賞招工；一天清晨，科隆比耶的老工頭小約瑟夫帶著一隊衣衫襤褸、目光呆滯如夢行者般的『工人』前來登記，問其姓名皆不應答。那不是活人，是可憐的還魂屍——約瑟夫與妻子克魯瓦昂絲把他們從安息的墳墓裡拖出，為其在烈日下作奴；眾所周知還魂屍絕不可沾鹽與肉，故克魯瓦昂絲另起一鍋，其食淡而無味。

sensitivity.note: The canonical modern zombie narrative (Seabrook 1929, event of 1918); presented as legend told by a named informant. The sensationalist frame of the source is noted; no recipes or practical details beyond the folklore.

passages.text: The spring of 1918 was a big cane season, and the factory, which had its own plantations, offered a bonus on the wages of new workers; soon heads of families and villages from the mountain and the plain came trailing their ragtag little armies — men, women, children trooping to the registration bureau and thence into the fields. One morning an old black headman, Ti Joseph of Colombier, appeared leading a band of ragged creatures who shuffled along behind him, staring dumbly, like people walking in a daze. As Joseph lined them up for registration they still stared, vacant-eyed like cattle, and made no reply when asked to give their names.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Seabrook, The Magic Island, ch. 'Black Sorcery' (1929); not verbatim.

passages.text: Joseph said they were ignorant people from the slopes of Morne-au-Diable, a roadless mountain district near the Dominican border, who did not understand the creole of the plains; they were frightened, he said, by the din and smoke of the great factory, but under his direction they would work hard in the fields — and the farther they were sent away from the noise and bustle of the railroad yards, the better. Better indeed: for these were not living men and women but poor unhappy zombies whom Joseph and his wife Croyance had dragged from their peaceful graves to slave for him in the sun — and if by chance a brother or father of the dead should see and recognize them, Joseph knew that it would be a very bad affair for him.

So they were assigned to distant fields beyond the crossroads, and camped there, keeping to themselves like any proper family or village group; but in the evening, when other little companies gathered each around its one big common pot of savory millet or plantains generously seasoned with dried fish and garlic, Croyance would tend two pots upon the fire — for as every one knows, the zombies must never be permitted to taste salt or meat. So the food prepared for them was tasteless and unseasoned; and as the zombies toiled day after day dumbly in the sun, Joseph sometimes beat them to make them move faster, but Croyance began to pity the poor dead creatures who should be at rest — and pitied them in the evenings when she dished out their flat, tasteless bouillie.

title.en: Salted Tablettes: the Zombies Remember Their Graves
title.zh: 加了鹽的花生糖：還魂屍歸墳

region.en: Cul-de-Sac cane fields and Morne-au-Diable, Haiti
region.zh: 海地庫爾德薩克蔗田與魔難山

texts.period: Haitian legend, event of 1918; recorded 1927-1929; published 2024 (published 2026)

source.work: William B. Seabrook, 'The Magic Island' (1929), ch. 'Black Sorcery' — the Fete-Dieu ending of the Hasco story

summary.en: On the day of the great feast Croyance, pitying her dead drudges once more, bought tablettes — 'not salted or seasoned, they are sweet, and can do no harm just this once.' But the baker had salted the pistache nuts before stirring them into the rapadou; and as the zombies tasted the salt, they knew that they were dead, made a dreadful outcry, arose, and turned their faces toward the mountain. No one dared to stop them, for they were corpses walking in the sunlight; and at their own village in the twilight they shuffled past fathers, wives, mothers who screamed and begged them to stay, up the path to the graveyard, and each before his own empty grave clawed the stones and earth to enter it again — and as their cold hands touched the earth of their own graves, they fell and lay there, rotting carrion.
summary.zh: 大節之日，克魯瓦昂絲再度憐憫這些亡者苦工，買來花生糖——『沒鹽沒料，是甜的，就這一次無妨』。誰知糖販在拌入糖漿前先給花生加了鹽；還魂屍一嘗到鹽，便知自己已死，發出可怖的哀號，起身轉向群山。無人敢攔——那是行走在日光下的屍體。薄暮時分，他們踏著碎步經過認出親人、哭喊挽留的村人，走上通往墓園的小徑，在各自空墳前刨掘石土欲入；冰冷的手觸到自家墳土的一刻，他們倒下，橫陳為腐肉。

sensitivity.note: Sequel of the Hasco narrative; the salt-taste rule is folklore-level. Source is Seabrook's popular-ethnography; the melodrama is his, the folk logic (salt releases the dead) is the tellers'.

passages.text: As Croyance sat with her savory dried herring and biscuit baked with salt and soda, and her provision of clairin in the tin cup by her side, she pitied the zombies who had worked so faithfully for Joseph in the cane fields and who now had nothing, while all the other groups around were feasting; and as she pitied them a woman passed, crying, 'Tablettes! Tablettes pistaches! Trois pour dix cobs!' — tablettes are a sort of candy, in shape and size like cookies, made of brown cane sugar, sometimes with pistaches, which in Haiti are peanuts.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Seabrook, The Magic Island, ch. 'Black Sorcery' (1929); not verbatim.

passages.text: And Croyance thought, 'These tablettes are not salted or seasoned, they are sweet, and can do no harm to the zombies just this once.' So she untied the corner of her kerchief, took out a coin — a gourdon, the quarter of a gourde — and bought some of the tablettes, which she broke in halves and divided among the zombies, who began sucking and mumbling them in their mouths. But the baker of the tablettes had salted the pistache nuts before stirring them into the rapadou, and as the zombies tasted the salt, they knew that they were dead, and made a dreadful outcry, and arose and turned their faces toward the mountain.

No one dared to stop them, for they were corpses walking in the sunlight, and they themselves and all the people knew that they were corpses; and they disappeared toward the mountain. When later they drew near their own village on the slopes of Morne-au-Diable — these dead men and women walking single file in the twilight, with no soul leading them or daring to follow — the people of their village, holding their hamboche in the market-place, saw them drawing closer, and recognized among them fathers, brothers, wives and daughters whom they had buried months before. Most of them knew at once the truth, that these were zombies who had been dragged dead from their graves; but others hoped that a blessed miracle had taken place on this Fete Dieu, and rushed forward to take them in their arms and welcome them.

But the zombies shuffled through the market-place, recognizing neither father nor wife nor mother; and as they turned leftward up the path leading to the graveyard, a woman whose daughter was in the procession of the dead threw herself screaming before the girl's shuffling feet and begged her to stay — but the grave-cold feet of the daughter and the feet of the other dead shuffled over her and onward. As they approached the graveyard they began to shuffle faster and rushed among the graves, and each before his own empty grave began clawing at the stones and earth to enter it again; and as their cold hands touched the earth of their own graves, they fell and lay there, rotting carrion.

title.en: Why the Peasants Build Tombs: Polynice's Apology
title.zh: 為何農人築石墓：波利尼斯的辯白

source.work: William B. Seabrook, 'The Magic Island' (1929), ch. 'Black Sorcery' (Constant Polynice on tombs, graves beside the road, and the night-watch with shotguns)

summary.en: Polynice, the rationalist friend, would not call it superstition: why do you suppose that even the poorest peasants, when they can, bury their dead beneath solid tombs of masonry? Why do they bury them so often in their own yards, close to the doorway? Why, so often, do you see a tomb set close beside a busy road where people are always passing? It is to assure the poor unhappy dead such protection as we can — and for his own brother, killed as everyone knew, he and Osmann kept four nights of watch in the peristyle with shotguns, until they were sure the body had begun to rot.
summary.zh: 理性友人波利尼斯不肯稱之迷信：為何連最窮的農人也要把亡者葬入堅固的石砌墓穴？為何常葬在自家院中、緊挨門口？為何墓塚總立於行人絡繹的大路旁？——這是為那些可憐而不幸的死者盡我們所能的保護。至於他那位死因眾人皆知的弟弟，他與奧斯曼在祭亭持獵槍守了四夜，直到確信屍身已開始腐爛為止。

sensitivity.note: Haitian funerary-protective practices described by a named informant; the watch described is a protective vigil, recorded as folkloric fact from the published source.

passages.text: The zombie, Polynice's neighbors said, is neither a ghost nor yet a person who has been raised like Lazarus from the dead: the zombie is a soulless human corpse, still dead, but taken from the grave and endowed by sorcery with a mechanical semblance of life — a dead body which is made to walk and act and move as if it were alive. People who have the power to do this go to a fresh grave, dig up the body before it has had time to rot, galvanize it into movement, and make of it a servant or slave, occasionally for the commission of some crime, more often simply as a drudge around the habitation or the farm.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Seabrook, ch. 'Black Sorcery' (1929); not verbatim.

passages.text: Seabrook asked Polynice to tell him something of the zombie superstition, that he might get at some idea of how it originated. His rational friend was deeply astonished, and put his hand in protest on his knee: 'Superstition? But I assure you that this of which you now speak is not a matter of superstition. Alas, these things — and other evil practices connected with the dead — exist. They exist to an extent that you whites do not dream of, though evidences are everywhere under your eyes.'

'Why do you suppose that even the poorest peasants, when they can, bury their dead beneath solid tombs of masonry? Why do they bury them so often in their own yards, close to the doorway? Why, so often, do you see a tomb or grave set close beside a busy road or footpath where people are always passing? It is to assure the poor unhappy dead such protection as we can.' He would take Seabrook in the morning to see the grave of his brother, killed as everyone knew: open space all round it, close beside the trail which everybody passes — and through four nights Polynice and Osmann had watched in the peristyle with shotguns, for at that time both his dead brother and he had bitter enemies, until they were sure the body had begun to rot.
